The null coalescing operator (??) is equivalent to isset($a) ? $a : $b, so it does not raise warnings for undefined variables.
The echo statement with commas concatenates the strings 'a' and 'b' and outputs 'ab'.
In PHP, print is an operator that returns the integer 1, so it can be used within expressions, unlike echo which returns nothing.
The Elvis operator ($a ?: $b) returns the left operand when it is truthy, and the right operand when it is falsy.
In PHP, the concatenation operator (.) has lower precedence than + and -, so expressions like 'a' . 1 + 2 are parsed as 'a' . (1 + 2).
The ** operator in PHP is right-associative, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512, not (2 ** 3) ** 2 = 64.
Concatenation has higher precedence than addition, so it parses as ('sum: ' . 2) + 3, which is 'sum: 2' + 3, and in PHP 8 the string 'sum: 2' converts to 0, giving 0 + 3 = 3.
With ===, arrays must have the same key/value pairs in the same order to be considered equal; it is == that ignores order.
In PHP, loose comparison (==) treats false as 0, so 0 == false evaluates to true.
In PHP 8, when comparing a non-numeric string to an integer, the integer is cast to a string, so 'abc' == 0 becomes 'abc' == '0' which is false.
In PHP, null == 0, null == '', and null == false all evaluate to true under loose comparison (==).
PHP's (int) cast reads numeric characters from the start of the string and stops at the first non-numeric character, so '42abc' becomes 42.
PHP coerces the numeric string '5' to an integer when used with the + operator, so 5 + 5 = 10.
In PHP, casting false to a string results in an empty string "", not "0".
Due to floating point precision, 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004, which is not strictly identical (===) to 0.3.
strrev() operates on a byte-by-byte basis, so it will incorrectly reverse multi-byte UTF-8 characters rather than treating them as single code points.
str_contains() returns true because 'world' is a substring of 'Hello world'.
str_pad() can pad on the right (default), left, or both sides using the $pad_type parameter (STR_PAD_RIGHT, STR_PAD_LEFT, STR_PAD_BOTH).
By default, trim() removes spaces, tabs, newlines (\n, \r), NUL bytes, and vertical tabs from both ends of a string.
In UTF-8, 'é' takes 2 bytes, so 'héllo' is 1+2+1+1+1 = 6 bytes.
substr with a negative start position counts from the end, so -3 starts at 'c' and returns 'cdef'.
ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character uppercased; it does not modify the original string in place.
Heredoc supports variable interpolation while nowdoc (delimited by single quotes) treats the content as a plain string with no interpolation.
sort() reindexes the array with sequential numeric keys, losing the original key-to-value associations; use asort() to preserve them.
PHP automatically converts string keys that represent valid non-negative integers into integer keys.
The third parameter $strict of in_array() defaults to false, meaning it uses loose comparison (==) by default, not strict (===).
Without a callback, array_filter() defaults to casting each value to a boolean and removes all falsy values (false, 0, '0', '', null, false, empty array).
The $preserve_keys parameter of array_slice() defaults to false, so keys are reindexed by default.
array_slice with offset 1 and length 2 returns the two elements starting at index 1, which are 20 and 30.
PHP array addition keeps left-side values for duplicate keys, so the result is ['a' => 1, 'b' => 2], which has 2 elements.
Since PHP 8.1, the spread operator in array literals supports arrays with string keys (previously it only worked with integer keys).
Named arguments can be combined with argument unpacking in a single call, as long as the named arguments come before the unpacking (e.g., foo(a: 1, ...$args)).
In PHP, anonymous functions (closures) do not automatically capture variables from the outer scope; they must be explicitly imported using the 'use' keyword.
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments actually passed to the function (3), not the number declared in the signature (1).
Arrow functions (fn) in PHP always have a single-expression body with implicit return; curly braces and multiple statements are used by anonymous functions (closures), not arrow functions.
PHP arrow functions (fn) automatically capture outer variables by value without needing a 'use' clause.
A static closure in PHP does not bind $this, so it cannot access the current object context unless $this is explicitly passed via use.
The closure captures $x by value at creation time (5), so later reassignment to 7 doesn't affect the captured value.
In PHP's coercive (weak) typing mode, the string '5' is automatically converted to the integer 5 when passed to an int parameter.

Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing constructor parameters to be automatically promoted to properties using visibility modifiers like 'private', 'public', or 'protected'.
In PHP, the 'final' keyword before a method declaration prevents it from being overridden in any subclass.
In PHP, the 'final' keyword on a method prevents it from being overridden in any subclass.
Private properties in a parent class are not accessible in a subclass; only public and protected properties are.
A private method in the parent class is not visible to the child, so the child is free to declare a method with the same name and any visibility without conflict.
__get() is also called when accessing inaccessible (protected/private) properties, not only non-existent ones.
Reassigning an already-initialized readonly property throws a ReadonlyPropertyException, which is a subclass of Error.
PHP interfaces can declare constants, which are implicitly public.
In PHP, the instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a specific class or interface.
Since PHP 8.0, interfaces can declare static methods, optionally with a default implementation.
The instanceof operator checks both class inheritance and interface implementation, so an object that implements an interface will return true for instanceof that interface.
Interface methods in PHP are always abstract and cannot have a body/implementation, unlike trait methods which can have concrete implementations.
In PHP, abstract methods can be declared as either public or protected, but not private.
The enum Foo has three cases (A, B, C), so Foo::cases() returns an array of 3 elements.
In PHP, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError extends Error, not Exception; both Error and Exception are siblings that implement Throwable, so catch(Exception) will not catch TypeError.
The @ operator suppresses errors (warnings, notices, etc.) but does not suppress exceptions; exceptions will still be thrown and propagate up the call stack.
intdiv(5, 0) throws a DivisionByZeroError in PHP 7+, which is a subclass of ArithmeticError.
The finally block always executes whether or not an exception is caught; it runs before the exception propagates further up the call stack.
An exception thrown in a finally block actually overrides/replaces any exception from the try or catch block, so it does have an effect on the result.
Shutdown functions registered via register_shutdown_function() are called when the script terminates, including when exit or die is invoked.
The 'use' statement is a compile-time aliasing directive that simply maps a short name to a fully qualified class name; it does not trigger autoloading or load the class file.
In PHP, you use 'use function' to import a function from a namespace, e.g., 'use function MyNamespace\myFunction;'.
PSR-4 strips the mapped prefix 'App\' from the FQCN, converts the remaining namespace segments to directory names, and appends the class name with .php extension.
Composer's vendor/autoload.php ultimately includes autoload_real.php which calls spl_autoload_register() to register the autoloader function.
__NAMESPACE__ is a magic constant that returns the current namespace name (or an empty string if in the global namespace).
An unqualified class name in 'new' is resolved relative to the current namespace first, falling back to the global namespace only if not found locally.
PSR-4 maps the remaining namespace (Model\User) to the relative path src/Model/User.php by replacing backslashes with directory separators.
PHP allows a use statement inside a function body, and the alias then only applies within that function's scope.
In PHP, arrays are value types and are copied on assignment (with copy-on-write optimization), unlike objects which use handle semantics.
In PHP, arrays are copied by value on assignment, so modifying $b does not affect $a, which still contains only 2 elements.
In PHP, global variables are not accessible within a function's local scope unless explicitly brought in via global, $GLOBALS, or passed as parameters.
Since $GLOBALS is an array of references to global variables, unset($GLOBALS['x']) removes the global variable for the entire script, not just the current function scope.
The function takes the parameter by reference (&$x), so the increment modifies the original variable $n from 5 to 6.

PHP's foreach iterates over a fixed set of keys determined at loop start, but values are read from the live array at each iteration, so modifications made in earlier iterations are visible in later ones.
A static property belongs to the class itself, so there is only one copy shared across all instances.
In PHP, a boolean key true is cast to the integer 1, so it is stored as an int, not as a bool.
Since PHP 5.5, generators support a return value that can be retrieved by calling $gen->getReturn() after the generator has completed.
In PHP, calling rewind() on a fully consumed generator restarts it from the beginning, re-executing the generator function so it can be traversed again.
PHP has the yield construct but no yield from construct; yield from is a Python feature.
Calling a generator function returns a Generator object, so get_class() returns the string 'Generator'.
The generator yields 1, 2, 3 from the array, so iterator_to_array produces a 3-element array, and count returns 3.
SplStack implements a LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) structure, while SplQueue implements a FIFO (First-In, First-Out) queue.
ArrayIterator is an SPL class that wraps an array and implements the Iterator interface, enabling traversal via foreach or iterator methods.
ArrayObject implements the Traversable interface (via Iterator), so it can be traversed with foreach.
password_hash() automatically generates a random salt and embeds it in the resulting hash string; there is no parameter to pass a separate salt.
In PHP 8, PASSWORD_DEFAULT is equivalent to PASSWORD_BCRYPT (or PASSWORD_ARGON2ID in PHP 8.4), not md5.
password_verify returns true when the given password matches the provided hash, and here we are verifying 'secret' against its own hash.
strip_tags() removes HTML/XML tags from a string, which helps mitigate XSS, but SQL injection is prevented by using prepared statements or proper SQL escaping, not by stripping tags.

session_regenerate_id() creates a new session ID while preserving session data, which is the standard defense against session fixation attacks by invalidating any old ID an attacker may have captured before login.
php_sapi_name() is the built-in PHP function that returns the current SAPI name, such as 'cli', 'fpm-fcgi', or 'apache2'.
session_destroy() only removes the session data on the server; the PHPSESSID cookie in the browser must be explicitly deleted with setcookie() by setting its expiry to a past time.
The $_SESSION array is only populated with stored session data after session_start() is called; without it, it is either undefined or an empty array.
get_class() on an anonymous class returns a string starting with 'class@anonymous' followed by the file and line number where it was defined.
Traits in PHP can declare constants, which become accessible to any class that uses the trait.
In PHP, casting any object to bool always results in true, including new Exception('x').
array_find() was introduced in PHP 7.4 as a convenience function for finding the first element in an array that matches a condition.
Property hooks (allowing get/set logic directly in a property declaration) were introduced in PHP 8.4.
Asymmetric visibility (e.g., public private(set) string $name) is a new feature introduced in PHP 8.4, allowing different read and write access levels for properties.
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.4 to mark function results that must not be ignored.
The pipe operator (|>) was introduced in PHP 8.4.
The clone-with syntax (clone($obj, ['x' => 1])) was proposed as an RFC but was never accepted into any released PHP version.
array_first() and array_last() were introduced as new array functions in PHP 8.4.
The RFC for Partial Function Application v2 was adopted for PHP 9.0.
The clamp_v2 RFC (which reintroduced the clamp() function after the original was removed from PHP 8.3) was implemented in PHP 8.4.
The Context Managers RFC (in its revised/accepted form) was adopted for PHP 8.5, which is scheduled for release in November 2025, so by 2026-11-06 it is already in effect.
The Bound-Erased Generic Types RFC was voted down (declined) during the PHP 2026 voting cycle.
While ZTS (Zend Thread Safety) is available as a build option in PHP, no RFC to enable it by default has been adopted.
PHP has no native generics or parameterized types as of PHP 8.5; developers rely on docblock annotations and static analysis tools instead.
PHP follows a November release cycle; PHP 8.6's GA is 2026-11-19, so on 2026-11-06 the latest stable would indeed be 8.5.
PHP 6 was never officially released; its planned features were merged into PHP 7.0, which followed directly after PHP 5.6.
The Deprecation Attribute RFC was rejected for PHP 8.4, falling just short of the 75% approval threshold.
